analysis.one_liner: Taxes wages above $250,000 for Social Security and boosts benefits for low earners, students, and widows.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the 115th Congress; it sat in four House committees from June 2017 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have applied Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000 a year, while keeping the tax unchanged for the roughly 94% of workers whose earnings fall under the existing cap. The new revenue would fund several benefit increases: a minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for long-career low-wage workers, larger benefits for widows and widowers, cost-of-living adjustments measured by an inflation index for seniors, and extended benefits for children of covered workers through age 23 while in school. It also prevented higher Social Security checks from pushing people off SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low-wage workers, who would get a minimum benefit pegged to the federal poverty line scaled by years worked; widows and widowers, who would get an alternate, often larger benefit amount; full-time students through age 23, who would keep receiving child benefits from a retired, disabled, or deceased parent; and current beneficiaries generally, whose annual cost-of-living adjustment would be tied to an inflation index built for seniors' spending patterns.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to every dollar of wages up to $250,000 and taxes income above $250,000, closing the gap in coverage between the old $127,200 cap and the new threshold and lifting the cap entirely above that [S2] [S3].
Guarantees a minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline, scaled from 6.25% for workers with 11 years of coverage up to 125% for 30 or more years of work [S3].
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the spending patterns of older households [S2] [S3].
Extends child benefits to full-time students through age 23, up from the existing age-19 limit, and includes college in the definition of eligible schooling [S2] [S3].
Provides an alternate, generally larger benefit formula for widows and widowers, calculated as the greater of the deceased worker's benefit or 75% of the combined amounts [S3].
Counts increased Social Security checks as capped at pre-bill levels for SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP eligibility, so higher benefits cannot strip people of other aid [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and high-income self-employed people, who would pay the 12.4% payroll tax on earnings between the old cap and $250,000, plus the tax on income above that; their employers pay the matching half on wages up to $250,000. Because only earnings above $250,000 count in the benefit formula (and then at only 2% of excess average earnings), most of the new revenue exceeds the new benefits credited to those earners, so the money largely goes back out to other beneficiaries.

drawbacks.text: Self-employed professionals and business owners pay both the employee and employer halves of the payroll tax, so a self-employed person earning well over $250,000 would owe the full 12.4% on all earnings up to that threshold, a materially larger tax bill [S3].

Raising the tax on high wages partially breaks the historical link between what top earners pay in and what they get out of Social Security, an objection critics of cap-raising proposals have long raised, though the bill partially answers it by crediting 2% of excess earnings toward benefits [S3].
Employers would owe the matching payroll-tax share on salaries between the old cap and $250,000, a new cost on high-wage payrolls that some employers could pass back through lower pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall narrowly on high earners and their employers, while the gains go to the people the program most underprotects: long-career low-wage workers, widows, and students of deceased or disabled parents. The main design tradeoff is the reduced contribution-benefit linkage for top earners, which the bill softens but does not eliminate. The bill is straightforwardly financed: new payroll tax revenue covers the new spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and a Social Security subcommittee in June 2017, and no committee ever acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Al Lawson of Florida introduced the bill on June 8, 2017 with 15 original Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3].

The House referred it to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees, with subcommittee referrals to Social Security, Health, and Railroads following within days [S5].
No committee markup, hearing action, or floor vote followed; the bill's action history ends with the June 20, 2017 subcommittee referral [S5].
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill died without a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners who would have paid the new payroll tax on wages above the old cap were spared the cost. Social Security's long-term financing shortfall was left unaddressed, and low earners, widows, and students gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners; the bill died unvoted

sides.party_line_note: All 20 original sponsors and all 19 additional cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% payroll tax on earnings up to $250,000 and on income above it, the main funding source for the benefit increases. Their cost directly pays for benefits to low-wage workers and survivors.
Employers would owe the matching payroll-tax share on wages between the old cap and $250,000, a new labor cost concentrated in industries with high salaries.
